doc.title: Joey Morant interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 2, 2013

chapter: Reflections on jazz, race and education
title: Can anyone improvise, and white musicians in jazz and R&B
summary: He argues all life is improvisation and that environment, not ability, kept white players from jazz and R&B.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You are talking about — you are an imaginative man I think. And it makes me wonder when I see — you know there’s a famous jazz improv method called “Anyone Can Improvise.”

Well I’m improvising all the time. We improvise when I’m sitting in the chair, if I pull my coat, it’s all improvisation. If I play with my fingers, you improvise all the time. Maybe not in music. But that is what you do in music. And music you fold your arms, you cross your legs, you straighten out your knees so you can relax, you think about your wife, if you’ve got a girlfriend you think about her too. So it’s all improvisation. When you want to turn it into music it now has to gel into one musical definition. So that’s when your character — you have to be able to control your character so you can push it out through the concept phrasings of the song. Like [sings] from the bottom of my heart, dear/I apologize. Billy Eckstine. This is it. “I Apologize” Billy Eckstine. So anybody can improvise if they either figure out the way or you show them the way. Because when I was growing up white musicians didn’t play jazz that well. Not because they couldn’t, not because they couldn’t, they were in an environment that didn’t condone it. They said whites can’t play R&B and funk, well whites are some of the funkiest players there are today. Michael McDonald is that the guy? Who’s the other guy? Oh Lord, with the raspy voice?
Michael McDonald, that’s another one. See? Linda: Michael Bolton?
